What is Splunk and how did you use it?

A platform for collecting, indexing, searching and visualizing machine data: logs, metrics, events. In a project you use it for production debugging (searching by traceId or error), dashboards (error rate, latency), alerts (for example, more than 50 5xx responses in 5 minutes triggers PagerDuty or Slack), and audit and security analysis. 💡 Have a real incident story ready: "we found the root cause by searching by traceId…"
Main Splunk components?

Universal Forwarder: a lightweight agent that ships logs. Heavy Forwarder: can parse and filter before sending. Indexer: parses, indexes and stores data. Search Head: the UI and the search engine. Deployment Server: manages forwarder configs. Cluster Manager (formerly Cluster Master): manages indexer clustering and replication. HEC: an HTTP Event Collector that accepts events directly from apps.
Common SPL commands?

search, stats (count, avg, sum, dc, perc95), timechart, chart, table, fields, rex (regex field extraction), eval (computed fields), where, sort, head/tail, dedup, top/rare, transaction, join, lookup, spath (JSON).
stats vs eventstats vs streamstats vs transaction?

stats aggregates and returns only the summary rows. eventstats adds the aggregate as a field to every event. streamstats computes running aggregates in event order. transaction groups related events into one (by id, startswith or endswith). It's slower, so prefer stats where you can.
Index vs sourcetype vs source vs host?

index: the logical store, with its own retention and access control (prod, dev). sourcetype: the data format, which determines parsing (access_combined, json). source: the file path or input. host: the machine the data came from. Always filter by index and time first, for performance.
How should applications log for Splunk?

Use structured JSON logs (Logback or Log4j2 JSON encoder) with timestamp, level, service, traceId, spanId and userId. Don't log secrets or PII. Use the right log levels. Put correlation ids in MDC. Send to stdout in Kubernetes, picked up by a forwarder or the Splunk OTel collector, or send directly to HEC.
How do you create alerts and dashboards?

Save a search, then choose Save As → Alert. Pick scheduled or real-time, set a trigger condition (number of results greater than N) and an action (email, webhook, Slack, PagerDuty), and add throttling. For dashboards, use Dashboard Studio panels built from saved searches, with time pickers and drilldowns.
Splunk vs ELK stack?

Splunk is commercial (licensed by ingest volume), enterprise-ready and easy to use, with powerful SPL. ELK (Elasticsearch + Logstash/Beats + Kibana) is open source and cheaper but takes more operational effort. Alternatives: Grafana Loki, Datadog, New Relic.
Explain what happens from a line being written to it showing up in a search.

- The app writes a log line to a file.
- The Universal Forwarder notices it, tags it with host, source and sourcetype, and sends blocks over TCP 9997.
- The indexer's pipeline breaks the stream into events, finds the timestamp (_time), and applies masking and routing rules.
- The event goes into the hot bucket: compressed into rawdata, with its terms in the tsidx file.
- A search head sends the search to the indexers. Each checks bucket time ranges, bloom filters, and tsidx, reads matching raw events, extracts fields, and returns results.
The usual delay is seconds. A larger gap between _indextime and _time shows a forwarder or queue problem.
Index-time vs search-time processing?

Index time covers what is stored: event breaking, timestamp, default fields, masking, routing, and any indexed fields. Changing it only affects new data. Search time covers what you see: field extraction, aliases, calculated fields, lookups, tags, event types. These apply to all data right away. Splunk is designed as schema on read, so you put as much as possible at search time.
Universal Forwarder vs Heavy Forwarder: when do you need the heavy one?

Use the UF by default, since it is light and does minimal processing. Use an HF when you need to parse or filter before the indexers, for instance routing events to different indexes or clusters, dropping noise to save licence, masking at the edge, or running add-ons that pull data from APIs. The HF is a full Splunk instance, so it costs more resources and parsing work happens there.
Multi-line stack traces appear as separate events. How do you fix this?

Set line breaking in props.conf for the sourcetype, on the first full instance (indexer or HF): SHOULD_LINEMERGE=false and a LINE_BREAKER with a lookahead for the timestamp. This is faster than leaving line merging enabled with BREAK_ONLY_BEFORE. A better long-term fix is JSON logging, so the stack trace is one field. New settings only affect new data. Long traces may also hit TRUNCATE.
Events show the wrong time. What are the likely causes?

Splunk found the wrong timestamp or the wrong zone. Set TIME_PREFIX, TIME_FORMAT and MAX_TIMESTAMP_LOOKAHEAD. Set TZ for the sourcetype or host if logs have no offset. Check for events far in the future or past, since these land in odd buckets and retention behaves strangely. Search with index=x | eval lag=_indextime-_time to see the problem, and check DateParserVerbose messages in _internal. Fixing old events requires re-indexing.
stats vs chart vs timechart?

stats gives a table, grouped by any number of fields. chart gives a two-dimensional table: over one field, by a second. timechart is chart with _time as the x-axis, automatic bucketing, and zeros for empty buckets. A top-level timechart ... by field keeps the top 10 series and groups the rest as OTHER, unless you set limit=0 or useother=f.
join vs stats vs lookup for combining data?

Use stats ... by key over a combined base search whenever possible. It is distributed, has no subsearch limits and handles large data. Use lookup when the other side is reference data. Use join only for small subsearches, and be aware of the limits on rows and time: truncation is silent, so counts may be wrong. Default join is an inner join, and it keeps only the first match on the right side unless you set max=0.
dedup vs stats latest(); what's the trap in dedup?

dedup field keeps the first event per value, in search order (normally newest first), and drops the rest. It also drops events that do not have the field, unless you add keepempty=true. stats latest(x) by key does a similar job in a distributed way and is usually faster. Only use dedup when you need the whole event.
where vs search in the pipeline?

search matches terms and fields with wildcards, and the values have search semantics. where takes an eval expression, so you can compare two fields (where a > b), which search cannot do, and call functions (where match(uri, "regex")). With where, a bare word means a field, so a string needs double quotes. A common bug is where status=ERROR, which compares to a field named ERROR.
What are multivalue fields?

A field holding several values in one event, created by values(), rex max_match=0, split or JSON arrays. Functions: mvcount, mvindex, mvfilter, mvjoin, mvzip. mvexpand field creates one row per value, which you need before counting by that value. mvexpand is memory-limited, so filter first.
How do you find the slowest 1% of requests per endpoint?

index=prod sourcetype=access_logs earliest=-1h
| eval path=replace(uri_path, "/\d+", "/{id}")
| eventstats perc99(ms) as p99 by path
| where ms >= p99
| table _time path ms traceId host | sort -ms
eventstats keeps the raw rows and adds the group value. So each event can be compared with its own group, and you keep the traceId for follow-up. stats would lose the events.
Find users who started checkout but did not finish.

index=prod (event=checkout_started OR event=checkout_completed) earliest=-1h
| stats values(event) as steps, min(_time) as started by sessionId
| where mvcount(steps)=1 AND steps="checkout_started"
| eval waiting=round((now()-started)/60,1) | sort -waiting
This is the pattern for detecting a missing event. transaction ... keepevicted=true and looking for closed_txn=0 works too, but costs more.
How do you calculate an error rate and compare it to last week?

index=prod sourcetype=access_logs earliest=-7d@h latest=@h
| timechart span=1h count(eval(status>=500)) as errors, count as total
| eval rate=round(errors/total*100,2)
| fields _time rate
| timewrap 1day series=short
Or compare two windows with appendcols. Dividing by a count of 0 gives null, which is fine for charts, but test it in alerts.
A dashboard is slow. How do you fix it?

- Open the Job Inspector for the slowest panel and see which phase costs the most.
- Tighten time and add index and sourcetype.
- Use one base search with post-process searches, rather than many similar ones.
- Replace join or transaction with stats.
- Use tstats on an accelerated data model, or schedule the search and load the cached result with loadjob or a saved report.
- Check that panels do not all refresh at once.
Why was my alert missed or fired late?

Common causes: the scheduled search was skipped because the search head hit its concurrency limit (check index=_internal sourcetype=scheduler status=skipped); the search window ends at now, so late-arriving events are missed; the schedule and window do not line up, leaving gaps; throttling suppressed it; or the mail action failed (check python.log). Use windows offset by a minute or more, and overlap them only if a throttle handles duplicates.
How would you reduce Splunk licence use?

Licence (in the common ingest model) counts raw data indexed per day. Find the biggest sources from license_usage.log. Turn off DEBUG logs in production, and stop logging full request bodies. Filter noise before indexing by sending it to nullQueue with props.conf and transforms.conf on an indexer or HF. Shorten JSON keys. Note that retention does not change licence use, as it counts ingest, but retention does affect storage costs.
# props.conf
[access_logs]
TRANSFORMS-drop = drop_health
# transforms.conf
[drop_health]
REGEX = GET /actuator/health
DEST_KEY = queue
FORMAT = nullQueue
How do you mask sensitive data?

Best: do not log it, by redacting in the app's logging layer. As a safety net at index time, use SEDCMD in props.conf, or a transforms.conf rule that rewrites _raw, on the first parsing tier. Search-time masking only hides data from view, and it stays on disk. Once stored unmasked, the data must be deleted and re-ingested. Restrict access to sensitive indexes by role, and audit it with index=_audit.
What's a knowledge object? Name some.

A user-defined item that adds meaning to data at search time: field extractions, calculated fields, field aliases, lookups, event types (a saved search as a label), tags, macros (a reusable SPL fragment, invoked with backticks), data models, workflow actions. They live in apps and have sharing permissions (private, app, global). A macro keeps long common filters in one place.
What's in the internal indexes?

_internal holds Splunk's own logs (splunkd, metrics, scheduler, license usage). _audit records user activity and searches. _introspection records resource use. _configtracker tracks changes to configuration files on recent versions. They are used for checking whether a forwarder is sending, why searches are skipped, and who ran what. For example, index=_internal sourcetype=splunkd component=Metrics group=tcpin_connections shows connected forwarders.
A forwarder's logs aren't appearing. How do you debug it?

- Check the data is not just in another index or time range: search index=* host=theHost earliest=-1d.
- On the host: splunk list monitor and splunk list forward-server, and is the process running?
- Read $SPLUNK_HOME/var/log/splunk/splunkd.log for connection errors and for TailReader messages.
- Check file permissions for the user running the UF.
- Check the path pattern in inputs.conf with splunk btool inputs list --debug.
- Look for blocked queues on the indexers, and network access to 9997.
- A file rotated with identical header bytes can be skipped, since the CRC of its start matches a seen file; crcSalt or initCrcLength addresses this.
What is btool? How are config files merged?

Splunk merges all .conf files by precedence across system/local, apps/*/local, apps/*/default and system/default. Never edit default. splunk btool props list order_app --debug shows the effective setting and which file set it. It is the key tool when a setting seems ignored.
What's an indexer cluster's RF and SF, and what happens when a peer fails?

RF is how many raw-data copies exist, SF how many are immediately searchable. When a peer fails, the cluster manager reassigns primaries, and tells other peers to make new copies to restore RF and SF. Searches continue while the cluster is "search factor met". Data forwarded to the failed peer is handled by automatic load balancing to the others. A multi-site cluster keeps copies per data centre.
Scenario: production latency jumped at 14:05. Walk through your investigation.

- Confirm scope: timechart span=1m perc95(ms) by service, to find the first affected service.
- Check it by host and endpoint, to see whether it is one instance, one path or everything.
- Check changes: deployment logs, restarts ("Started OrderApplication"), config changes.
- Check error patterns from 14:00 to 14:10: timeouts, HikariPool exhaustion, GC, Kafka rebalance.
- Take one slow traceId, follow it across services and find the slow gap between timestamps.
- Correlate with metrics (database, CPU) in Grafana or Splunk Observability.
- Write down the timeline, save the searches as an alert so that recurrence is caught sooner.
Scenario: design logging for 50 microservices in Kubernetes.

Standardise a JSON log format with timestamp, level, service, version, env, traceId, spanId, message. Log to stdout. Run the Splunk OpenTelemetry Collector as a DaemonSet to send to a HEC tier behind a load balancer. Use one index per environment or data sensitivity, since permissions and retention are per index. Use a sourcetype per format, not per service. Pick a retention per index. Use a shared logging library so teams get MDC and redaction by default. Budget ingest by team, with dashboards and alerts. Keep metrics and traces in their own tools, and link them by traceId.
What's a good log line? What should not be logged?

A good line is machine-parsable and answers who, what, outcome and how long: {"level":"WARN","service":"order","traceId":"...","event":"payment_retry","orderId":"A-42","attempt":2,"ms":840}. Use stable event names and fields rather than free text, as dashboards depend on them. Do not log passwords, tokens, card numbers, personal data or full payloads. Avoid logging an exception at every layer, as it inflates error counts. Choose levels with care: ERROR means a person should look, WARN a recoverable oddity, INFO a business event, DEBUG off in production.
How do you restrict which teams can see which logs in Splunk?

Put data with different sensitivity in different indexes, then give each role access only to the indexes it needs via srchIndexesAllowed in authorize.conf (or the Roles UI). Map SAML/LDAP groups to those roles. Role search filters can narrow further, and knowledge objects have private/app/global sharing permissions. 💡 Index is the boundary for both access and retention, so design indexes around those two needs, not around applications alone.
What is the CIM and why do data models matter?

The Common Information Model normalises field names across sources (for example user, src, action) so one search or dashboard works for logs from many vendors. Data models define a structured view on top of CIM-compliant data, and when accelerated they store summaries that tstats can query very fast. Security tools like Splunk Enterprise Security rely on CIM data models heavily.
App vs add-on (TA) in Splunk?

An app delivers a user experience: dashboards, saved searches, reports and navigation. A technology add-on has no UI; it contains inputs, line-breaking/timestamp rules and field extractions for a specific data source (for example a TA for Linux or AWS logs). Install the TA where its settings apply: inputs on forwarders, index-time parsing on indexers or heavy forwarders, search-time extractions on search heads.
How would you alert on an abnormal error spike instead of a fixed threshold?

Build a baseline: bucket counts with bin/timechart, compute avg and stdev over the last week with eventstats, and alert when the current bucket exceeds, say, avg + 3*stdev. Better still, compare the same hour last week (timewrap) to handle daily seasonality, or alert on the error rate rather than the raw count so traffic growth doesn't fire it. Add throttling so one incident creates one alert.
Splunk vs Prometheus/Grafana — do you need both?

They solve different problems. Splunk indexes logs/events and is great for searching arbitrary text, investigations and audit. Prometheus stores numeric time-series metrics scraped from endpoints such as Spring Boot's /actuator/prometheus; it is cheap and fast for dashboards and alerting on rates, latencies and saturation. Many teams use metrics for "is something wrong?" and logs for "why?", with a shared trace ID to jump between them. Splunk can store metrics too (metrics indexes, mstats), but cost usually favours a metrics system for high-volume numbers.
